speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Chairman, I move, "That the total sum allocated to Head O of the Estimates be reduced by $100." S+3M, subsidies Medisave, MediShield and MediFund, is one of our nation's quiet triumphs.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It has protected generations of Singaporeans from catastrophic bills.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It has embedded shared responsibility, personal ownership and equity.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Today, our dominant risks are chronic, progressive, community-based: diabetes, dementia, frailty, mental health conditions.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: They do not bankrupt a family overnight, but they exhaust a family slowly.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Dementia day care costs about $63 per session.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: At my Woodlands Meet-the-People Sessions, I often hear two concerns: one, "why can't I use my Medisave?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It's my money"; and two, "I already used up all my MediSave for chronic care".

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Mrs L, a retiree, cares for her husband with early dementia, while managing her own diabetes.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: She told me, "I saved all my life.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Why does it still feel like my money isn't enough to stay independent?" Or K, 24, pays out of pocket for mental health care because her condition is not officially chronic. "I'm probably going to need this for the rest of my life.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: How is that not chronic?" These are the lived realities faced by our fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Incremental cap adjustments and coverage expansions help, but they do not fundamentally reshape incentives.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Our system still signals we pay more attention when you are already very sick.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Our lifestyle risks are rising faster than our population ages.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Healthier SG fully subsidises routine screenings and immunisation programmes.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Active-living infrastructure like parks, fitness corners, cycling paths, Active Ageing Centres and community health programmes encourage functional health.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Some seniors need physiotherapy to prevent a fall.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Some need home rehabilitation to prevent a re-admission.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Some need cognitive stimulation to prevent the onset of dementia.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Some adults need weight management programme to prevent diabetes progression.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Some youths need early mental health interventions to prevent a spiral.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: These are investments in independence, not discretionary lifestyle perks.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: S+3M must evolve, not just to pay bills, but to shape behaviour, support prevention and sustain independence.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Many schemes require three Activities of Daily Living (ADLs).

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Introduce an early intervention tier for "pre-frail" seniors – funding physiotherapy, balance training, and strength exercises.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: One month of rehab today can prevent a decade of nursing home care tomorrow.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: A treatable condition should never become a terminal one because someone hesitated over the cost.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Two households may have the same per capita household income (PCHI), but the one supporting elderly parents and young children carries a heavier burden.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Adjust subsidy tiers for households with multiple dependents.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Subsidies must be easy to use, visible and structured to encourage early preventive action.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Automatic enrolment, co-payment reductions, integrated Medisave bonuses and seamless digital claims are ways to nudge behaviour.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Let it fund chronic disease management, broader preventive screenings, evidence-based doctor-referred functional health or nutrition programmes, early rehabilitation after minor injuries or hospital stays, early interventions for dementia or frailty, expanded mental health support.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Keep the remainder MediSave core for major episodes.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Unused flex balances roll over, rewarding responsible early actions.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Bonuses can be awarded, tied to improvements in chronic disease management and functional assessments.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Together subsidies and MediSave flex nudge Singaporeans to act early, adhere to chronic care, and engage in preventive programmes.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Singaporeans get more flexibility while the systems preserve catastrophic coverage.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: MediShield Life remains for rare, high-cost hospitalisation, keeping premiums affordable.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Explore premium credits for preventive prescriptions if they are shown to save costs.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: MediFund remains the final safety net for those genuinely in need.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: S+3M actually has been a safety net catching us when we fall.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But in an ageing society, we need a springboard that keeps us standing, strong, independent and healthy.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We must adapt S+3M: financing not only healthcare, but health itself, not by abandoning the principles, but by fulfilling them fully.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is about spending earlier, so that we spend less later – financially, socially, emotionally.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And, Sir, none of these changes one thing.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The Government must do everything in its power to keep healthcare affordable and rein in healthcare inflation.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: If we get this right, we will not only treat illness.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Individuals matter, yes, but in Singapore, healthcare risk is shared.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: There is no such thing as a purely private health cost.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: When preventable illnesses rise, premiums rise, taxes rise.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Preventive care saves lives and reduces costs, but only if people participate.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: If prevention is essential, it should not depend on who remembers to click a link.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: And design does not sit with MOH alone.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: It is about what our children eat in school.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Whether our neighbourhoods invite movement or discourage it?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: The healthy choice must be the easy choice.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Healthier communities do not just happen by chance – they are designed.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: MOH has launched a programme to improve health in the North, and Woodlands, my Constituency, is piloting an integrated preventive health model.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: We have a diverse mix of seniors and families, the full range of housing types, strong community institutions, and opportunities to strengthen chronic care.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: With two hospitals, several polyclinics and Active Ageing Centres within easy reach, we can test how to bring care closer to home and refine integrated care team models.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: The pilot rests on four pillars: first, stronger referral pathways and chronic disease support.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Second, moving care closer to home, with smoother transitions; third, redesigning neighbourhoods so that the healthy choice is the easy choice; and fourth, activating communities as health advocates.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: But it cannot be policy on paper – it must be about real people, living healthier lives, every day.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: I therefore have two questions and three requests for the Minister.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: The questions: one, how will success be measured?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Two, what resources will be available for grassroots activation?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: The requests: ensure town-level care hubs are fully integrated and consistently staffed so residents can access services without delay; expand the scope of community-based care and caregiver support, to cover more conditions and families; and involve my residents directly in co-designing interventions so solutions reflect their real needs and let us avoid stigmatising any community.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Health outcomes are shaped by the systems – transport, food, work patterns as well as socio-economic factors, not moral failings.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: When she does not feel like cooking, there are plentiful healthy and affordable Halal options at Kampung Admiralty Hawker Centre.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: With care and support closer to home, her diabetes is under control and she stays independent.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: If we can redesign a town for health, we can redesign a nation.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: First, I declare my interest as managing director of a management consulting firm that works in AI and healthcare.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: AI in healthcare is often discussed in terms of use cases – detecting disease earlier, automating paperwork, predicting risk, personalised medicine.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: But today, I want to ask the Minister a bigger question: what is our ambition?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: If healthcare is truly a national AI mission, our goal cannot be incremental adoption.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: We must build a system – the infrastructure, the governance, the talent, the plumbing that lets AI transform care safely, effectively and at scale, with better outcomes for every patient in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Once we show that AI delivers real patient benefit safely and reliably at scale, Singapore will naturally move from adopter to a global leader in trusted healthcare AI.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: But infrastructure alone does not make us a leader.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Interoperability supports care delivery, but safe access for innovation and AI development, including with third parties, remains rather limited.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: One, stronger data frameworks – national data architecture, secure sandboxes, synthetic datasets, and federated learning that enable AI innovation without compromising patient privacy.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Two, interoperable systems that allow AI models to learn across institutions while keeping clinicians in control.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Three, governance rules: every AI recommendation must be explainable, auditable, accountable.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Clear innovation governance; top down or bottom up.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: On global collaboration, our stance must be clear: we welcome expertise, but only under frameworks that protect our data, preserve sovereignty, build local capability and benefit patients.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: We need national validation, certification and post-deployment monitoring – standards for bias, explainability and real-world performance, so patients and clinicians can trust every AI decision.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: We need professionals fluent in both clinical realities and machine learning.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: But Singapore must be a place where AI solutions are built, tested, certified and scaled safely, and where patient outcomes improve at every step.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Singapore must set the standards for trusted, safe and effective AI.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: With out-of-pocket expenses a consistent bugbear for many Singaporeans over the last few years, and the basic healthcare sum rising exponentially year-on-year, there is an expectation that the additional withdrawal limits that allow Central Provident Fund (CPF) members to use more of their MediSave money to service their IP premiums, are in need of a revision.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It cannot be reasonably expected that this number or the amount of money that can be used should remain the same after so many years.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Does the Ministry plan to review this in the immediate term?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The headline of an opinion piece last month in The Straits Times expressed a major anxiety of the health system succinctly: "Singapore as a super-aged society: can its health system cope?" The author, an academic with a specialty in public health, observed what is commonplace for many Singaporeans when they visit our public hospitals and healthcare institutions – a large number of seniors in wheelchairs, visibly frail, or struggling with mobility.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The assessment is that this number would be broadly adequate for the population's healthcare demands for the years to come.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The intersection of a rapidly ageing population and higher demand for healthcare services will bring the adequacy of the healthcare workforce into distinct focus and any shortages or perceived shortages will be reflected most acutely in service quality, waiting times for specialist care and waiting times to see a healthcare professional, amongst others.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In parallel, there are real concerns and worries about the welfare of our healthcare workers, from allied health professionals to nurses and doctors, in view of heavier patient loads that are anticipated.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Separately, the projected increase in healthcare manpower begs the question of how much allowance or buffer is being factored into the healthcare system, including in the event of Disease X type scenarios – a key lesson learned from the COVID-19 experience.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is a number which the Minister has said he expects to increase.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: First, what is the scope of the surge capacity when our healthcare system reaches the upper end of 156,000 healthcare workers?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Does the surge capacity account for an additional buffer of doctors, nurses and allied health workers?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Or is the surge capacity a case of restructuring processes to do more with less in times of surge demands?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If it is the latter, for how long can the healthcare system operate at an optimum level of performance?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Second, does the Ministry plan to increase the range of publicly reportable statistics from what is currently available to waiting times at hospital emergency departments, polyclinics and specialist outpatient clinics, amongst others?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We should carefully track the capacity of the system to cope with the significant demands our demographic shift imposes on it.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is useful to remember that healthcare is a very unique public service.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Prime Minister identified healthcare as one of four national AI Missions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: AI indeed stands to inject new productivity possibilities into healthcare at the ecosystem level.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, at the level of a Singaporean who needs healthcare, what makes healthcare, healthcare, are the people – the doctors, the nurses, the allied health workers – who look after us when we are at our lowest.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In that context, the human touch and the personal connection will never be fully replaced by AI.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, if it means that our healthcare manpower in the years to come would require additional buffers, we should devote more fiscal resources towards it accordingly.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Dr Hamid Razak, you can take your two cuts together.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, for some Singaporeans, healthcare is not just confined to a bill.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Today, in this House, I want to share the story of a young Singaporean I met – Gwendalyn.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: In her early 20s, she was diagnosed with hereditary breast cancer.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: For a young cancer survivor, reconstruction is not cosmetic.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: There are many such Gwendalyns in our society today.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: People I speak about are those with hereditary risk of cancer.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Cancer care today is not only clinically complex, it is also financially and psychologically complex, especially for hereditary disease.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: So, the policy question is this: how do we support people who may not be sick today, but are clearly at elevated risk?

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: To that end, I would like to ask the Minister three broad questions.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: For example, in the case of Gwendalyn, if a mass was found on one breast and was found to be diseased, she undergoes mastectomy, what about the contralateral breast, which at current state is healthy but we know she carries the gene for breast cancer?

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: How can the system be seamless when caring for such individuals?

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Third, how do we strengthen survivorship pathways for young cancer patients, including psychological and social support, not just medical follow-up?

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, the test is not just about survival, but about how survivors can return to life.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, if hereditary cancers speak about how complex medical care is, then precision medicine tells us how intelligently we can respond to the challenge.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: At National University Health System (NUHS), the Centre for Healthy Longevity is building programmes that strengthen healthspan, not just treat illness, helping Singaporeans stay physically strong, cognitively sharp and metabolically well as we age.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This matters because the public demand is already there.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: People are seeking tests and optimisation outside the mainstream system.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: If our public pathways do not keep pace with the credible evidence, we risk two things – fragmented care with uneven quality, with widening inequality and a missed opportunity for Singapore to lead responsibly as a trusted regional centre.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: While we focus on taking care of our seniors and our elderly, which is important, the key question as we go about with our society is how do we optimise every Singaporean, regardless of age, to reach the highest potential health for their age?

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: So, Mr Chairman, Sir, may I ask the Minister three questions.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Third, how will we enable responsible innovation so that we remain evidence-based, future-ready and trusted, so that our policies can keep pace as the evidence emerge, and we do not wait for two to three years after the evidence has already become mainstream?

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Because the goal obviously is not just longer life.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The goal is delayed decline, preserved independence and dignified ageing.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I recognise and agree that there is a need for cost containment and management of insurance premiums.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On cancer specifically, MOH has made significant moves.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Three months ago, MOH announced a key policy change in hospitalisation insurance.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In one of them, he appeared to suggest that the only use of the existing rider was to reduce the deductible and co-insurance, and the public should consider whether they need a rider at all.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, my understanding is that riders may be essential, especially to cancer patients for other reasons.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First, riders help to pay for costly cancer drugs that are not on the Cancer Drug List, which could be critical for the patient's treatment.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Second, there is the issue of loss limits.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Without a rider, the patient would need to pay 10% of a hospitalisation bill without any cap.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The second more general issue relates to preventive medical interventions which may not be covered by insurance.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: A young breast cancer patient wrote about her plight to The Straits Times' forum page on 28 January.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: She followed the doctor's advice to remove both breasts even though only one was cancerous.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Her hospitalisation insurance covered surgery for the cancerous breast, but only partially for the non-cancerous one.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In April last year, MOH recognised that the line between preventive and diagnostic care was increasingly nuanced, particularly in cases involving genetic predisposition to serious conditions, like breast cancer.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: MOH mentioned that it would issue claim rules to guide practitioners on breast-related surgical claims later that year.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: What is the present status of this review?

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Mr Chairman, adult children are often the default caregivers for ageing parents.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is a good thing when adult children want their parents to stay with them, even better when the parents are active and in pink of health.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Nonetheless, some Singaporeans feel penalised for doing the right thing.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is what I call the filial care paradox.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The parents are now seen as part of a higher-income household or living in a housing type with a higher annual value.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am not suggesting that we abandon means testing in our healthcare and social assistance architecture.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But we can recognise caregiving households more explicitly.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is a grace period so that the seniors' benefits do not immediately disappear when caregiving arrangements change.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Third, explore functional needs assessment, where we assess the social assistance based on actual needs rather than looking solely at household income or housing type.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Mr Chairman, when adult children bring their ageing parents into their home and care for them, we should give them more support, not less.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Those of us who have fallen seriously ill at one point or another will be keenly aware of how our healthcare expenditures are lumpy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: That is, we may go one year without any medical expenses, but in another year, we may end up spending far more than we would have anticipated.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is often the case even for chronic conditions since new diagnostic or treatment procedures may only be required on occasion.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The reality of spending spikes is corroborated by more systematic research in health economics.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, it is also well-known that end-of-life spending tends to be elevated.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Patients tend to spend most in the final years of their life.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: MediSave currently faces annual withdrawal limits of several types of care.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: One does not wish for patient to exhaust their MediSave funds, especially knowing that most of their care costs will indeed be incurred at the tail end.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But this is problematic because the policy is not aligned with the lumpy nature of medical expenses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It also glosses over the role that insurance, including public ones, such as MediShield Life, plays in such instances, since these are more likely to pay out for major illnesses that will otherwise exhaust their MediSave.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Actual data from the CPF supports this notion that there may be excess for saving in our MediSave accounts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There are two ways to better calibrate MediSave limits.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This will allow those who incur larger than expected bills to not have to rely on out-of-pocket funds, which, especially for retirees, are frequently paid for by working-age family members so as to be able to top up their medical expenses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While nobody can accurately predict when an individual's demise might be, we can rely on aggregate statistics on mortality by gender to adjust claim limits accordingly.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is intuitive to allow more spending at later ages where individuals' health will have deteriorated more.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This would ensure any condition requiring long-term management can be subsidised under CHAS and paid for via MediSave.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Even for conditions on the Chronic Disease Management Programme list, the MediSave 500/700 withdrawal limits can be restrictive.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I last raised this issue in 2021 and the Senior Minister of State argued that the risk of overconsumption necessitates these caps.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, how does this apply to public healthcare institutions, where salaried doctors follow strict protocols?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The real risk is not overconsumption but undertreatment.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: When patients are forced to choose between their cash and their care, some may choose to skip medications or appointments to save money.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Self-rationing today can lead to a massive bill tomorrow and emergency hospitalisation.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This is a tremendous cost to both the individual patients and the healthcare system.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Has the Ministry assessed the clinical cost of medical non-compliance caused by rigid MediSave withdrawal limits?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Singaporeans want to be self-reliant and not have to appeal for subsidies or medical assistance.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Chairman, I declare my interest as Chairman of the Mental Health Board at the NHG Health.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I rise to make the case that Singapore should position the Institute of Mental Health (IMH) as the true Centre of Excellence in psychiatric treatment and care, and to ask the Minister three questions towards that goal.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: IMH is our only dedicated psychiatric hospital, housing our most experienced psychiatrists and specialised teams.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Yet it remains stretched across the full spectrum of acuity.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: If we are serious about building a Centre of Excellence, we must free IMH to focus on what it does best – leading research, training the next generation of mental health professionals and managing our most complex cases.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Is IMH better resourced than our acute hospitals to handle complex psychiatric patients?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: And a Centre of Excellence should not merely treat; it should set clinical standards across our entire healthcare system and across all three public healthcare clusters.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: How is IMH’s specialist expertise being leveraged across the three clusters to uplift psychiatric treatment and care in all our acute hospitals and in the community, so that IMH is not bogged down by excessive referrals beyond what they can handle effectively and efficiently.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Will the Minister share data on polyclinic acceptance rates for patients discharged from IMH and acute hospitals with psychiatric diagnoses?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: A Centre of Excellence cannot function if its beds are occupied by patients ready for step-down care.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)

text: I'm sober and I have stayed away from pornography for the past five years." What happens inside us?

text: Or question whether that even counts as sobriety?

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Queenstown)
text: While we are prepared to discuss substance addictions openly, we remain uneasy when the addiction is behavioural, private and sexual in nature.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Queenstown)
text: Pornography addiction is often dismissed as indulgence or simply part of growing up in a digital age.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Queenstown)
text: Yet for some individuals, consumption becomes compulsive, distressing and disruptive to daily life.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Queenstown)
text: To be sure, dopamine is not the enemy.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Queenstown)
text: It is a neurotransmitter essential to how our brains function.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Queenstown)
text: It motivates us, reinforces learning and gives us satisfaction after effort and achievement.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Queenstown)
text: But dopamine also plays a central role in addiction.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Queenstown)
text: When certain substances or behaviours repeatedly trigger intense reward signals, the brain adapts.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Queenstown)
text: Over time, the brain begins to prioritise the behaviour associated with that reward.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Queenstown)
text: What begins as voluntary can, for some, become difficult to control.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Queenstown)
text: Addictive substances, such as drugs and alcohol, are well recognised for this effect.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Queenstown)
text: Increasingly, research has examined behavioural addictions, including gambling disorder, gaming disorder and compulsive sexual behaviours, which engage similar reward pathways.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Queenstown)
text: Pornography today is instant, anonymous, inexpensive and available through smartphones at any hour.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Queenstown)
text: There are no physical barriers and few natural stopping points.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Queenstown)
text: For a subset of individuals, repeated exposure and escalating consumption can entrench patterns that are hard to reverse.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Queenstown)
text: Some international studies suggest that problematic pornography use may affect figures in the low double digits, depending on definitions used.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Queenstown)
text: Methodologies differ, but the emerging literature suggests this is not an isolated phenomenon.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Queenstown)
text: Even if prevalence in Singapore is lower, the absolute number affected could still be significant.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Queenstown)
text: We must also situate this issue within the broader digital ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Queenstown)
text: Social media notifications, online gaming achievements, gambling wins, auto-play streaming.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Queenstown)
text: Our attention economy is engineered to keep us engaged.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Queenstown)
text: It is one of many digital stimuli competing for our attention.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Queenstown)
text: But it differs in one important aspect: it can shape expectations about intimacy, about consent and about relationships.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Queenstown)
text: When exposure begins early, often before emotional maturity has developed, the lessons absorbed may not reflect mutual respect or healthy communication.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Queenstown)
text: In Singapore, conversations about sexuality are often cautious.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Queenstown)
text: When guidance is absent, young people may turn to the Internet as their primary educator, and we all know that the Internet is not designed to teach values.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Queenstown)
text: What once required effort, patience and real human interaction now arrives instantly on screens engineered to capture attention.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Queenstown)
text: If our public health response focuses only on treatment after harm, we will always be reacting to damage, rather than building resilience.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Queenstown)
text: When relationships deteriorate and emotional health declines, the impact is not confined to the private sphere.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Queenstown)
text: So, as policy-makers concerned with mental health, we cannot ignore emerging behavioural addictions simply because they are uncomfortable to discuss.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Queenstown)

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Queenstown)
text: Family dynamics, peer influence, trauma and broader cultural factors all play roles.

text: With support from We Care, Dale learned to trace his triggers, sit with discomfort and name his emotions instead of numbing them.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Queenstown)
text: Recovery was slow and imperfect but deeply human.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Queenstown)
text: It is a story of early exposure, silent conditioning, secrecy, shame and courage.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Queenstown)
text: Behind the label of "addict" is a human being, once a curious boy, trapped in silence, who needed understanding, community and support.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Queenstown)
text: If we are serious about addressing this issue, we must move from discomfort to evidence-based strategy.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Queenstown)
text: We need to understand prevalence, mental health associations, relational impacts and risk factors.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Queenstown)
text: With evidence, we can calibrate responses proportionately and responsibly.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Queenstown)
text: Young people need emotional literacy, digital resilience and grounded understanding of consent and healthy intimacy.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Queenstown)
text: Parents too may need support navigating conversations in a rapidly evolving digital landscape.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Queenstown)
text: If exposure is increasingly common, then equipping youths and their families with tools to interpret what they encounter responsibly becomes essential.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Queenstown)
text: Those who seek help should encounter accessible and timely support.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Queenstown)
text: It is about how young people form expectations about relationships.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Queenstown)
text: It is about how couples build trust over time.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Queenstown)
text: If we want strong families and resilient youths, then we cannot treat this problem as unspeakable.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Queenstown)
text: We cannot eliminate temptation, but we should not normalise harm.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Queenstown)
text: If technology has industrialised temptation, then our response must be to industrialise resilience: thoughtfully, proportionately, with care.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Queenstown)
text: Let us not hesitate simply because the subject is uncomfortable.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Queenstown)
text: Let us choose evidence over denial, courage over avoidance and support over stigma.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Queenstown)
text: Because the question before us is not whether this issue exists, but whether we can address it together head on.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: While we have prepared for an ageing population for many years, we need to accelerate our efforts across infrastructure, systems and people.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Today, many Singaporeans acquire caregiving knowledge and skills only when their parents or loved ones fall ill, become bedridden or need help with the activities of daily living.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: We should consider large-scale training of caregivers ahead of time as most adult Singaporeans will at some point become caregivers to family members or supervise caregivers at home.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Those who are trained to a certain proficiency can form a community caregiving corps.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: It is costly both to the state and individuals for patients to rely only on hospitals or clinics for basic services, such as injections, wound care or physiotherapy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Where appropriate, self-care and community-based support can complement institutional healthcare services, with a caregiving corps within each neighbourhood playing a part.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Services provided by the caregiving corps could include basic clinical care, personal care, therapy, psychosocial support and related assistance within clearly defined care protocols.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: The corps could include young seniors trained to support older seniors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: This would keep younger seniors active and engaged in the community, while at the same time, earning some supplemental income.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Caregivers in this programme would need to periodically refresh their skills, with competencies validated or accredited by healthcare institutions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: An online directory or mobile application could help residents find the help they need within their neighbourhood.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: We should similarly scale up training for domestic helpers ahead of demand.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: This would expand caregiving capacity across households, relieve pressure on the formal healthcare system and equip helpers with skills that enhance their employability and earning potential.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Community caregiving should be complemented by scaling up the deployment of technology within homes to help monitor the physical and emotional well-being of seniors, particularly those living alone.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Such tools would enable care workers or small neighbourhood teams to keep track of seniors and coordinate services, like community nursing, cleaning and transport to polyclinics.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Chairman, Singapore will become a super-aged society this year.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: This means that many Singaporeans will become caregivers at some point.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Our families, especially those who are middle income and sandwiched between young and old, will come under increasing pressure and strain.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Our women, who traditionally shoulder a more of the caregiving load, will be disproportionately impacted.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Further, through Age Well Singapore programme, we will help more seniors age well in the community.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: I have a few clarifications and would like to provide some suggestions on how we can refresh our Caregiver Support Action Plan in the next bound.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: First, what are the critical gaps in accessibility, affordability and quality of eldercare services that our middle-income families continue to face?

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: And what are the Ministry's plans to address these gaps?

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Addressing these gaps are important, so that working caregivers can continue working with peace of mind that their loved ones are well-cared for.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Family members who have mental health conditions or degenerative diseases, such as dementia, which is becoming more common, who may require high supervision but may not necessarily qualify for the three ADL criteria today.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Ideally, our life-span and our health-span should be closer.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: The concern that we live long but not well, is real.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Preventive healthcare is therefore vital to help our seniors reduce years of bad health and increase their quality of life in retirement.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: The Healthier SG Programme was launched to address this.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: However, I wish to advocate for the Ministry to do more and expand the range of preventative healthcare for our seniors.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: I will address two areas related to the Healthier SG Programme.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: We can expect the numbers to have increased and continue to increase in our ageing society.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Dementia is both debilitating and scary for seniors.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Poor bone health on the other hand, leads to deteriorating mobility and overall health in seniors, especially after a fall.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Both conditions take a tremendous toll on caregivers in the family.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Our seniors can face loneliness, grief, loss of purpose after retirement and the anxiety of declining health and independence.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: They also belong to a generation that may not often have the vocabulary to convey their mental well-being needs.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: With the increased emphasis on mental wellness, I would like to enquire on the status and ambit of this roll-out, particularly for our seniors and whether it would expand to other mental ailments.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Relatedly, I would also like to ask the Minister if he can provide our Active Ageing Centre Teams or even our Silver Generation Ambassadors, structured training in basic mental health first aid, so they can be first responders for emotional well-being in the community.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Visiting hospitals can often be an unpleasant experience, unless one is expecting a newborn.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: I want to address the challenges faced by many individuals, including my own experiences.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: As many are aware, when our elderly parents go for check-ups, they often require the assistance of their children.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: This process typically involves several tests, followed by consultation with a doctor regarding the next steps.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: I am aware that certain medical institutions offer video consultations.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: If I may propose that we utilise video calls to all hospitals and polyclinics and minimise waiting times and the hassle of hospital visits for simple updates.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: While I understand that some situations necessitate in person consultation, technology can significantly enhance the overall experience.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: By leveraging available technology, and now with AI, we can support especially the sandwich generation who juggle responsibilities for both their children and ageing parents.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: These caregivers often need to take time off from work for medical appointments and the lengthy waits sometimes over an hour; even two or three hours for brief updates can be frustrating.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, when my son had a football injury, we faced a similar situation.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: After waiting for over an hour, the doctor's update lasted for only for five to 10 minutes.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: Such interaction could be efficiently handled through video calls, which would also allow for real time updates on waiting times for treatments.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: The time and energy required for parents to attend these appointments can be overwhelming.

speaker: Mr Azhar Othman (Nominated Member)
text: I hope the Ministry considers implementing solution that facilitate a similar experience for those caring for both elderly parents and young children.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, I address the Minister on two fronts: strengthening social prescribing and optimising clinical capacity.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: We have built the parts of a better healthcare system, including social programmes, trained professionals and enrolment infrastructure.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: This limits the match to what matters to the patient and when we match well, they go.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: To match well, our care teams need a maintained real time directory of what exists in each neighbourhood.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: SingHealth Community Hospitals are the world's first World Health Organization Collaborating Centre for Social Prescribing with trained well being coordinators and proven outcomes.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: The Living Asset Map developed by SingHealth Community Hospitals with the Ministry of Culture, Community and Youth and Singapore Land Authority already captures community assets in real time, updated by practitioners on the ground.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Map the full ecosystem: arts, culture, heritage, nature, sports, informal community partners and interest groups and resource link workers to close the last mile.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Some may worry that widening referrals could overwhelm social partners.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: That is precisely why the ask is not an open floodgate, but a mapped, maintained and matched pathway resourced to sustain.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: But a pathway only works if patients stay long enough to use it.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: From what I see in practice, not all enrolled patients have completed even a first health plan.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: They have signed up, but never sat down.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Some will ask, is this not about patient choice?

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: No one loses the right to see another doctor.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: What changes is the default that one doctor, one team knows you.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Subsidies encouraged the first step, but a subsidy is not a relationship.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Without activation, patients drift and the social needs that only surface over time never do.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: We must continuously learn what make patients stay.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: The Ministry consulted widely before Healthier SG launched; continue that rigour.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: And resource are providers GPs and polyclinics alike to keep them.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Team-based care is the direction our system has committed to, our clusters have built the frameworks.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: We have trained nurses, pharmacists and allied health professionals to practise at the top of licence.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: But without familiarity, many patients choose otherwise and never benefit.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: What we hear on the ground suggests utilisation is not where it should be.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: If we build capacity and fail to activate it, the system pays twice: once to train; once when the doctor does the same work.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: As we prepare to inject more professionals into the system, getting this right is not optional.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: It is the condition for that investment to pay off.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Some will say patient preference for doctors is too strong, but care is growing more complex and no single pair of hands can manage it alone.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: That is why we have trained these professionals in the first place, not to replace the doctor, but to surround the patient.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Preference follows familiarity, but familiarity requires introductions and reminders.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: That is the national effort I asked for.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: The industry changed the default to structured team functioning.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: The clusters can build the frameworks, but shifting public expectation requires more than any single cluster can do alone.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: My third ask: lead that national effort to help Singaporeans understand and trust the care that nurses, pharmacists and allied health professionals provide.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Support the clusters in ensuring investment in training translates into care.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Three asks each with a metric, each building on what already exists.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, let me show you what this looks like when all three asks work.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Because she stays, her doctor learns her story.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Once stable, her nurse takes over, adjusting medications, coaching on lifestyle and function preservation.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: She remains well for a year, then two, then her blood pressure climbs.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: The care coordinator calls and brings her back.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: She tells the doctor that her husband died last year.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: He refers her through the social prescribing pathway and a link worker to a gardening group three blocks away.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: She needed a care team alongside her and a community partner that mattered to her.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Mr Chairman, in healthcare, technology is often discussed in terms of speed, scale and innovation.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is about whether they can return home.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In stroke rehabilitation, I often meet patients who ask a single question, "Will I be able to walk independently again?" They are not asking about algorithms or processing power.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: They are asking about dignity and whether their lives can resume some sense of normalcy.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As Singapore becomes a super-aged society, the question before us is not whether we embrace technology in healthcare.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The question is whether we deploy it in ways that strengthen independence, reinforce our workforce and preserve sustainability in the long term.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Three shifts will determine whether technology becomes transformational or merely incremental.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Singaporeans are living longer, but longevity without independence places strain on families, caregivers and the system itself.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But the true measure of progress is not technological sophistication.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is whether fewer seniors lose mobility, whether fewer families experience preventable emergencies, whether more Singaporeans can age confidently in their own homes.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: When we intervene earlier, we preserve independence longer.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is social stability and fiscal resilience in an ageing nation.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Healthcare will always be human, but our professionals today face rising clinical complexity alongside administrative burden and coordination demands.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Clinical decision-support systems can synthesise complex patient histories.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Digital triage tools can prioritise risk more effectively.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This allows therapists to focus on assessment, clinical reasoning and patient engagement rather than repetitive supervision.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Technology must give clinicians back time, not take professional judgement away.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If technology reduces cognitive overload and unnecessary administrative friction, it sustains morale, protects professional standards and helps us retain the workforce our system depends on.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: A sustainable healthcare system ultimately depends on a sustainable healthcare workforce.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Healthcare systems often measure performance in terms of waiting times, bed occupancy and utilisation volumes.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Can I climb the stairs to my flat?

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Can I live independently without becoming a burden to my family?

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Technology should improve outcomes that patients feel, not just metrics we report.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Mr Chairman, Singapore's strength has never been blind adoption of new tools.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Because ultimately, the goal of healthcare is not activity, it is dignity across the life cycle.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If we deploy technology wisely, we will ensure that Singapore's healthcare system remains advanced and not only that, but also humane, resilient and sustainable.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Mr Chairman, my speech covers the Ministry's initiatives to bring care closer to the community, how we are strengthening our environment and ecosystem for healthy living and our efforts to improve our population's health.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: As our society ages, improving our population's health and preventive care is critical for longer, healthier lives.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We have embedded preventive healthcare into the community through Healthier SG and AgeWell SG to support residents while they are still relatively young and healthy, and as they age.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: These care protocols will ensure evidence-based care is provided more consistently through Healthier SG general practitioners (GPs).

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Ms Mariam Jaafar also spoke about improving community health, in particular the north region.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Our data shows that in the north, the prevalence of diabetes and hypertension is above the national average, and residents engage in less physical activity.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: While we continue to review reasons for these trends, we are simultaneously stepping up our preventive care efforts in the region.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: First, we will enhance the Community Health Posts (CHPs) in the town.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Thirdly, we will support residents to engage in healthy living activities by opening up community spaces for exercise programmes, introducing digital wayfinding in Healthy 365 and empowering local community health advocates.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: As seniors age, visiting polyclinics and hospitals can be difficult due to mobility issues.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Many also ignore symptoms that are not yet serious or urgent.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Consulting a healthcare professional early can lead to earlier identification of issues, which in turn leads to earlier intervention and better health outcomes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: These enhanced CHPs, which are located within Active Ageing Centres (AACs), will be opened once a week.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: These services are provided by NHG Health's community health teams comprising community nurses and health coaches, who will bring in pharmacists, dietitians and therapists based on residents' needs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: They also work closely with GPs in the region and healthcare professionals in hospitals to provide coordinated care for residents with chronic diseases and frailty.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: For example, residents with diabetes receive ongoing support at enhanced CHPs through glucose monitoring and personalised health counselling, with the community health teams regularly updating the residents' specialist doctor on their progress and any changes in their condition.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This ensures interventions can be made early if needed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: For seniors who are already at the AACs for programmes, they can also consult healthcare staff easily without needing to make a separate visit.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We have also noticed that some patients miss specialist appointments due to work schedules or limited mobility.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Starting with diabetes and asthma, selected patients can choose to receive specialist-supported outpatient care at an enhanced CHP through teleconsultation with the hospital care team.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Instead of travelling to Woodlands Hospital for their appointment, they will be able to see a health coach or nurse at the enhanced CHP to manage their condition and will receive support from the specialist doctor through teleconsultation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: With regular monitoring of health conditions, nurses are able to pick up early signs of poor control and work with specialist doctors for early treatment and help patients avoid unnecessary hospital admissions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Woodlands Hospital has also started rolling out teleconsultation for selected patients who have undergone colonoscopy screening with low-risk screening results.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Instead of making a trip to Woodlands Hospital, patients can choose to teleconsult their specialist doctor from anywhere, including at the CHP, if they need help.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This option will be further expanded to other specialties and procedures in Woodlands Hospital.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: With these services, patients will be better supported by the community care teams in their neighbourhood, while requiring fewer visits to Woodlands Hospital.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This will help patients access required care in a more flexible way, while working around other commitments.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This is expected to increase further as the initiative expands.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Even as we are bringing healthcare services closer to the community for greater accessibility, we agree with Ms Mariam Jaafar that health begins with individual choices and we can design a healthier ecosystem to support individuals to make better personal health choices in different settings.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: One key setting is the immediate neighbourhood that residents live in.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Health Promotion Board (HPB) conducted a study and found that residents are more likely to participate in health activities held in everyday surroundings that are accessible, green and fit seamlessly into their busy lives.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: They also value social experiences that are fun and community driven.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: These insights point to the need for a collaborative, ground-up approach with local community partners.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: They understand both residents' needs and preferences and the community spaces within the neighbourhood.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: They also play critical roles in facilitating access to neighbourhood facilities and spaces, encouraging participation in activities and building social connections that will make healthy living appealing and sustainable.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Thus, HPB will work with local community partners so that residents will find it easier to access and participate in healthy living activities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In tandem with holding more activities in the community, we will help residents explore and make greater use of existing neighbourhood amenities themselves.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Residents can continue to receive rewards when they track their participation via the Healthy 365 app.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Beyond the infrastructure, what will be key is the software – the networks and bond of the community.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We want residents to look out for one another and encourage relatives, neighbours and friends to participate in healthier lifestyles that will build healthier people and healthier towns.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: HPB will support local community stakeholders, who have deep understanding of residents' needs and community resources, to co-design healthy lifestyle programmes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This includes developing a citizen-centric playbook from June 2026 to help partners effectively plan relevant activities for residents.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Through collective ownership, residents will benefit from healthy lifestyle programmes and activities that are tailored to them.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We will also jointly monitor progress to continually refine and improve on the initiatives.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: HPB will explore how to expand successful elements to other towns.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Besides ground-up, community-led initiatives, we are looking at ways to mitigate lifestyle risk factors to improve the health of our people.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: One example is a cohort smoking ban or tobacco-free generation policy as mentioned by Ms He Ting Ru.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This means to restrict the access to all tobacco products for a specific birth cohort onwards.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Through our current multi-pronged approach of policy measures, public education and cessation support, we are making good progress in reducing the prevalence of smoking.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We are also continually reviewing our tobacco control policies, including the tobacco-free generation policy which some other countries are exploring.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Adopting a cohort smoking ban requires serious consideration.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We remain open to the policy and will study its effectiveness, impact and how it may be implemented in Singapore's context.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Ministry of Health (MOH) is focusing our attention on combating the scourge of vaping.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Hence, for now, we will continue to monitor international developments and learn from the experiences of other countries in how they implement a cohort smoking ban.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Mr Chairman, allow me to say a few words in Malay. :   Adopting healthier lifestyles is something that we need to work towards collectively in our community.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The National Population Health Survey 2024 showed that our Malay/Muslim community has some areas to improve on.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Chronic disease screening among Malays fell nearly 10 percentage points, from 64% in 2019 to 55% in 2024.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Breast cancer screening rates went down from 29% in 2019 to just 18% in 2024.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: When chronic conditions and cancer are not detected early, serious complications may arise, which will require more intensive and costly treatment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I understand that topics on health, such as screening, can be daunting.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Thus, it helps to be able to speak to trusted healthcare workers in a familiar setting to guide us along.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: A range of services, from general health advice and basic health assessments, to support for preventive health, disease management and post-discharge follow up will be provided.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We will tailor these services to our community's needs, for example, consultations can be conducted by community nurses and health coaches who are fluent in Malay to help minimise communication barriers, especially for seniors.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: NHG Health will also seek feedback from asatizahs to include faith-based guidance into health workshops.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This programme provides individual support in small group settings to help residents enroll in Healthier SG and book health screening appointments.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Thus, HPB will scale up Jom Check! to reach out and benefit more residents.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Small actions, like going for regular health screenings now, can avert bigger problems in future.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This is easier to do with Healthier SG, as eligible enrollees can enjoy special subsidies for Healthier SG screening tests.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This percentage is higher for those aged 60 and above, at approximately 70%.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Our community also registered the highest growth in enrolment over the past year.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: For those who have not yet enrolled, I highly encourage you to take that crucial step and enroll today.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This is a major concern, as obesity increases our risk for developing multiple chronic conditions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The National Nutrition Survey shows that calorie intake, as well as consumption of sweet foods and drinks, is highest among our community.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We also consume a high amount of saturated fat.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This could be due to the excessive use of cooking oil.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: However, I am confident that we can make small, sustainable changes that is in line with our lifestyle and culture.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Indeed, in our culture and religion, balance is important.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Taking care of our body is a sacred responsibility.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Let us reduce our intake of sugar, sodium and saturated fat and eat a healthy, balanced meal.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Government, together with MUIS, MENDAKI, PA MESRA under M3 and partners from the Jaga Kesihatan, Jaga Ummah network (JKJU), will continue to support efforts to enhance our community's health and well-being.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I am heartened when I see our community making steady progress.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We are now in the holy month of Ramadan which is an ideal time for our community to resolve to lead a healthier lifestyle.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We will continue to work with our partners to reach out to the community.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Come, let us all take the first step today and enrol in a health programme. : Mr Chairman, our goal is to ensure that the path to a healthier life is wide enough for everyone to walk on.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Through our initiatives, no one has to navigate their health journey alone.

speaker: The Minister of State for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: By working hand-in-hand with our community partners and residents, we can build a Singapore where healthy living is inclusive, accessible and a lived reality for every one of us.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Chairman, three years ago, in April 2023, I informed the House that Singapore would become a super-aged society in 2026 – this year.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is when 21% or more of our population will be 65 and above.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, if you consider, in June 2025, last year, already 20.7% of our population was 65 and above.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And that percentage has been going up by about one percentage point every year.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There was not a Singapore Civil Defence Force siren or anything.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It progresses quietly, with a real and profound impact.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And at MOH, we feel it very strongly in the hospitals, in the emergency department, in nursing homes, and we are doing our best to manage the workload and care for all our patients.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They have helped cushion the impact of this very profound demographic transition.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But arguably, the most complex task to prepare for an older population is to sustain and to transform the healthcare system.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These are the two topics I want to talk about today – sustain and transform.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Rising demand for care means the healthcare system must expand its capacity.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We will become bigger, which we are doing.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: However, meeting rising demand and running a larger system will cost more.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And if we do not manage this carefully, rising healthcare spending can strain public finances and household budgets alike.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In fact, if we are really extravagant, if we are not careful about it, it will cripple our system.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I think we need to start at the very top to ensure that the national healthcare bill is under control.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Otherwise, it is like the Titanic sinking, and you are pouring water out of the deck.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Ultimately, it is always paid by the people.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, a government can claim that "we provide cheap or even free healthcare".

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The truth is healthcare is never really free, even if patients do not pay anything at the point of delivery.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They will just pay in some other ways.

speaker: The Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: A sick nation that consumes healthcare indiscriminately will incur a large and wasteful bill and it will be very costly to the population, to the households, to the patients, to the people.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is a scatter chart of different countries and you can see Singapore is an outlier, in the bottom right corner.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The vertical axis measures how much the population spends on healthcare.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is an internationally accepted and generic measure of health outcomes.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And Singapore has one of the highest lifespans in the world.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
