text: But of course, beyond lifespan, there are many other measures of health outcomes and across all these measures, Singapore is comparable to or even better than many developed economies.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, how did we become an outlier like this?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think it has a lot to do with our S+3M healthcare financing system that Members are familiar with.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And MediSave is the linchpin of that system.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Singaporeans and our employers set aside part of our monthly income into MediSave.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The Government also provides top-ups from time to time for various segments of the population, and we did that again this Budget.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And we then use MediSave to co-pay directly for a small part of the cost of healthcare.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, even for a modest co-payment, it goes a long way to instil discipline and reduce unnecessary consumption on both the supply as well as the demand sides.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We do not have to look very far to imagine what happens when that discipline is eroded.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: You just look at private healthcare in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The discipline of co-payment was weakened because of overly generous insurance, including the IP riders.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As a result, private hospital bill sizes have been rising rapidly, and private insurance premiums have been escalating very quickly.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Once that genie is out of the bottle, it is difficult to put it back.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But it will not stop us from trying.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In our S+3M system, multiple payers pull their weight to pay for this national healthcare bill.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Apart from co-payment, we have insurance schemes like MediShield Life.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: A big part of it is also paid by charity dollars.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We thank all the donors and philanthropic organisations.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But the biggest proportion, about half. of the national healthcare bill is paid through tax revenues, redistributed as Government healthcare subsidies.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And beyond 2030, the Government's health budget will likely continue to grow.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We must ensure that the increase can be supported by economic growth and by rising tax revenues.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And at the same time, we must continue to maintain that discipline and avoid unsustainable levels of healthcare spending that we see elsewhere.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The next topic I want to talk about is transforming the healthcare system.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: A healthcare system for a young population is very different from one for an older population, for a super-aged society.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For a young person, sickness tends to be episodic.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: You are admitted to hospital, you get treatment, you get discharged and then you recover.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: On the other hand, an older person's care journey is complicated and continuous.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: When well, they need preventive care; when sick, they need coordinated care because they tend to have multiple conditions; post discharge, they need rehabilitative care and follow-up care in the community.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Good health is not a default; it is a continuous quest for an old person.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, from episodic hospital care, we now need continuous multi-disciplinary care across settings.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This shift is reflected in how we have allocated healthcare funding over time.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The chart on the left, the height of the chart is our Government healthcare budget in 2021.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Members can see that, overall, budget has increased by 1.5 times.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But I want to draw Members' attention to the composition.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: At the start of this decade, 2021, around three-quarters of our operational funding for the healthcare sector went towards acute hospital care – that is the white portion of the bar.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The remaining one-quarter was spent on aged care and population health, including preventive and primary care.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Over the same period, the share for population health grew from 14% to 19%.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: These shifts are driven largely by our national programmes, Healthier SG and Age Well SG.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think, almost certainly, the share of spending on aged care will grow further, because we need more nursing homes, senior care centres, rehabilitation services and hospice care.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As for population health, we do our best to maintain this share at around 19%.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: With total spending rising, maintaining the share alone requires a strong commitment to continue to invest in population health.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Chairman, today, my MOH colleagues and I will be speaking on further steps to transform healthcare and get ready for the future.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Senior Minister of State Koh will speak about manpower.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Senior Minister of State Tan Kiat How will speak about anchoring care in the community through technology.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And Members heard Minister of State Rahayu speaking about population health and preventive care, including what we are doing in the north, where prevalence of chronic diseases is higher.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There was a question by Ms Mariam Jaafar, she missed that part of the speech.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I should emphasise – this is in case she asks many clarifications later – preventive care and population health remain the overarching strategic thrust of what we are doing, anchored by Healthier SG and Age Well SG.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is at the core of healthcare transformation and MOH agrees with many of the points they have raised.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I will now speak about three new initiatives to support healthcare transformation.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The first common topic this whole Committee of Supply (COS) and Budget debate – AI, once again.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Ms Mariam Jaafar and Dr Choo Pei Ling spoke about how AI can strengthen healthcare delivery and we agree.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: When it comes to AI in healthcare, we are guided by two principles.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Clinicians remain in the loop and healthcare remains a profoundly human endeavour.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Two, we take a practical, use case approach.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: AI should not be a hammer looking for a nail, a solution looking for a problem.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We deploy AI where we know it will improve patient outcomes or the delivery of care, and where it can do so cost-effectively.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: One such use case is in health screening.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Around the world, many AI models have been trained to predict if a well person is likely to develop severe diseases in the near future.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If we use it appropriately and responsibly, such tools are very useful.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It helps the clinicians intervene earlier; it can delay or even prevent the onset of serious diseases.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: MOH has developed such a model for our local context using anonymised patient data.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We chose diabetes and high cholesterol because they are the key drivers of strokes and heart attacks, which affect 60 Singaporeans every day – every day, 60 Singaporeans either have a heart attack or a stroke.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If the tool flags a patient as high risk, the doctor may recommend more significant lifestyle adjustments and instead of three-yearly check-ups, maybe annual check-ups.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: These additional screenings will continue to be subsidised under Healthier SG.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The second initiative, I think is an exciting and significant one, and a breakthrough, which is to use genomics to strengthen preventive care.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: They shape our biological blueprint and indeed, many diseases are linked to our genetic characteristics.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But we need not be fatalistic about it.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: How we live, how we manage risk matters a lot.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, we do not go fumbling through our genetic blueprint, hunting for blemishes and possible mutations that we know little about.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It will create a lot of anxiety in all of us, and we will become a nation of hypochondriacs!

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, instead of shooting in the dark, we should focus on the parts of the blueprints that are illuminated by science.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This means taking a disease-specific approach, identifying genetic characteristics that we know drive certain diseases and for which we know there are established preventive interventions and treatment pathways.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is what we did for familial hypercholesterolemia (FH).

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: FH is a genetic condition that increases the risk of heart attacks even amongst young people.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The FH genetic testing programme offers subsidised genetic testing for individuals with abnormally high cholesterol levels.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And if they are tested positive, we will offer the same test to their immediate family members.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: By doing so, we try to identify as many individuals as we can in Singapore with the FH genetic mutation.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And then, we take steps to reduce their risk of future heart attacks and strokes.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We will now move on to our next genetic condition, which is hereditary breast and ovarian cancer (HBOC).

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In Singapore, it is estimated that one in 150 individuals carry a gene mutation, such as the BRCA1 or 2, that are associated with HBOC.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Such mutations substantially increase a woman's lifetime risk of developing breast and ovarian cancer.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: They will undergo genetic counselling before and after the test.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In addition to subsidies, the cost of the test can also be offset using MediSave.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For those found to have the mutation, they will be offered suitable preventive interventions.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Typically, this means more frequent breast MRIs or mammograms or oral medication.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Patients will ultimately decide, in consultation with their doctors, which intervention is appropriate.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Members may recall celebrity actress, Angelina Jolie, after she discovered she had the BRCA1 gene mutation, she underwent a double preventive mastectomy.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I came across women in Singapore who chose to undergo preventive mastectomy to reduce their risk of breast cancer, such as Ms Gwendalyn Too, and these women have demonstrated great courage.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Unfortunately, they lament that they cannot claim insurance for such surgeries, because MediShield Life generally does not cover prevention.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And it is designed to be so for a good reason.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is to keep coverage focused and premiums affordable.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Then private insurance takes dressing from MediShield Life.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Dr Hamid Razak and Ms Sylvia Lim asked about this.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In fact, Ms Stefanie Thio – she is the founder of the non-profit organisation SG Her Empowerment (SHE) – has raised this issue with me several times.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: With advances in medical science, the boundary between preventive and curative care is increasingly blurred.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If a high-risk individual is unable to undergo preventive mastectomy, she has a high chance of eventually needing cancer treatments, including a curative mastectomy to remove cancerous cells in her breast or cancerous tissue in her breast.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There is, hence, a case for MediShield Life to be judiciously extended to cover certain selected preventive surgeries.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We are prepared to do so when there is a clear clinical need, minimal risk of abuse, the procedure is suitable for risk-pooling, through insurance, and it does not financially burden the MediShield Life scheme.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I should add that breast reconstruction is also covered, no different from today.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This will better support women to harness genomics to better take care of their health.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think this is a meaningful policy change ahead of International Women's Day on 8 March.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The third initiative is to inject more flexibility in the use of MediSave to encourage early intervention and reduce downstream complications.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Assoc Prof James Lim was right to describe medical expenses as lumpy.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Indeed, it is very well documented that hospital expenses escalate almost like a vertical wall towards the end of life.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And so, even after accounting for inflation, the average Singaporean living up to their mid-80s spends almost four times as much on hospital expenses in the last 10 years of their life compared to the previous 10 years.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But that explains the existing design of the MediSave withdrawal system, and why the system is designed like that, why the scheme is designed like that.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It has higher limits for more complex treatments and longer hospital stays, and you can draw on it as and when you need it.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This meets the original objective of MediSave, which is to co-pay for major in-patient episodes, whether they happen unexpectedly or in old age.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: However, it is human nature to worry about present medical expenses rather than lumpy potential, unexpected or future hospital bills.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Hence, as a relief valve, we have schemes, like Flexi-MediSave and MediSave500/700, to provide flexibility for chronic disease management for scans, for dentist visits, and so forth, without overly diluting MediSave's original objective of catering for these big lumpy hospital bills in old age or during emergencies.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But the situation has changed since MediSave was implemented in 1984.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: At that time, people in Singapore lived to about 73 on average.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: On one hand, it continues to be important to preserve MediSave for big hospital bills.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: On the other hand, as people live longer, the need to spend on preventive care and chronic disease management also go up.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Hence, I can appreciate the repeated and various calls by Members to allow MediSave to be used more flexibly, to cover more chronic diseases, or as Mr Pritam Singh suggested, to pay for higher private insurance premiums.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But I also hold the realistic view that no matter how frequently MOH reviews the MediSave scheme, how much we liberalise and expand its usage, the public and Members of the House will continue to press me and MOH to liberalise the scheme every year during the COS and probably, outside of the COS.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is the karma of the scheme – because it is designed to be the linchpin of the healthcare financing system.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It must always navigate between present and future healthcare needs, between recurring disease management and the major hospitalisation episodes.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Using more balances for recurrent medical expenses means having less in the future when we are hospitalised and vice versa.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And when the tension becomes too severe, we will have to consider raising contribution rates so that you have a bigger pot to spend.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The tension is therefore deliberate and a design feature.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is a balance we must constantly and carefully manage, to ensure the system of co-payment is held together while ensuring affordability and keeping CPF contribution rates reasonable for everybody.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Hence, we continue to have ongoing, regular reviews to study where we can expand the use of MediSave and provide more flexible withdrawals.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This scheme helps patients pay for their recurring costs of managing conditions on the Chronic Disease Management Programme (CDMP).

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Cai Yinzhou and Mr Gerald Giam asked about this.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In addition, we are studying whether we can include other chronic conditions, such as eczema, in the CDMP.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: With the above enhancements, we will rename "MediSave500/700".

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Every time you change the limit, you change the name.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We will rename it to "MediSave Chronic and Preventive Care Scheme", to reflect its scope of coverage.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Before I end this section, let me address the question posed by Ms Sylvia Lim.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: She mentioned the role of riders in providing additional coverage for cancer treatments not on the Cancer Drug List (CDL).

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The objective of the recent changes to IP riders is to prevent over-erosion of co-payment because that sets off a "buffet syndrome" and then that leads to rapid escalation of private hospital bills.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: IP riders covering non-CDL drugs for outpatient treatment, do not contribute to this erosion and therefore, this feature will not be affected by the changes.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I should also point out that the changes to IP riders affect only new policy holders, but not existing policyholders.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We will always watch out for the cancer patients when we make changes to IP riders.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: (In Mandarin):   Two thousand twenty-six marks the year when Singapore enters the super-aged phase.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We should view this milestone with level-headedness and a calm mind, much like celebrating a birthday.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Whilst we are collectively a year older as a society, life continues as usual without sudden or dramatic changes.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Singapore has always prepared for rainy days and we have long been preparing for an ageing society.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Over the past decade, the Government has progressively adjusted policies across various domains with the goal of ensuring every Singaporean has support in old age, medical care when ill and a home to live in.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The most important point is to ensure that our people remain young at heart despite growing old physically.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Therefore, preventive healthcare has become the MOH's core policy focus.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Speaking of the MOH or "卫生部" in Chinese, I do have some thoughts on this Chinese name.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Strictly speaking, "卫生" is more commonly associated with hygiene, yet MOH does not manage hygiene matters.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Hygiene matters are managed by the Ministry of Sustainability and the Environment, which is helmed by Minister Grace Fu.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: However, from a medical perspective, everyone understands that the concept of "卫生" is about preventing, fighting and treating various infectious diseases, which remains an important mission of ours.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: However, the medical challenges of modern society differ from those of the past.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Non-infectious diseases, such as cancer, heart disease and diabetes now cause far more harm than infectious diseases.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: To better reflect MOH's core policy focus, we will change the Ministry's Chinese name to "保健卫生部", adding "healthcare" into the name.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: When our name reflects our core policy focus, the words and actions of the Ministry will naturally follow suit.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Some may ask whether changing MOH's Chinese name would cost a lot of money.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Please be assured that it will not, as most of our logos, legislation, documents, websites and so forth use only our English name.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The name change will mainly affect future media reports and the expenditure will be minimal, but the meaning it conveys is very important.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I have also just announced several new policies.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Second, we will begin providing subsidised genetic testing for hereditary breast and ovarian cancer for higher-risk women from the end of this year.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Third, we will use artificial intelligence (AI) to assist doctors in predicting individual's risk of developing chronic diseases, such as high cholesterol and diabetes.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For high-risk Singaporeans, we will encourage them to take preventive measures through Healthier SG.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Speaking of AI, over the past year, I have visited the US and China with the MOH team to study their experiences and practices in applying technology in healthcare.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In the US, we visited several renowned hospitals.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: When I asked them which AI application scenario was the most effective amongst all possibilities, they unanimously said that using AI to record patients' medical histories saves both time and effort and is the best application scenario.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Although the use case seems simple, it allows everyone to benefit from it.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It encourages everyone to accept new technology and understand that new technologies can help us, rather than threaten us.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In our public hospitals, we have already started using AI to document medical histories.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Our AI understands English, Mandarin, Malay, Tamil and Cantonese.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I am not sure why only Cantonese among the dialects but it is currently working hard to learn other dialects.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Someone once joked with me that the most experienced doctors will look at the person or the patient; experienced doctors will look at the illness; and less experienced doctors will look at the computers.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I believe that in the near future, with the help of AI, most doctors will be able to look at the person and not just at the computers.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This year, I also visited China and toured some hospitals and technology companies.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I found that Chinese hospitals are also boldly trying out new technologies and their courage to innovate is something worth learning from.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: However, we must also recognise that there are differences between China and Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Our transition to a super-aged society has been steady rather than dramatic.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It reflects deliberate, long-term planning, including transforming the healthcare system.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Indeed, healthcare transformation is fundamentally a long-term endeavour, not one sweeping reform.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is the accumulation of numerous small steps, each taken with judgement and purpose, each carefully planned and executed.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Chairman, it is my hope that this House continues to support our approach of long-term planning, long-term governance, to anticipate future challenges early and act before they overwhelm us.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If we do so, we need not fear being a super-aged society.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We can embrace it and we make the best of it.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Ultimately, it is not the percentage of Singaporeans above 65 that defines us.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We can exercise our wiser minds, to mourn less for what age takes away from us than what it leaves behind.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We are not just a super-aged society, but we are striving to be a super-healthy one as well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Mr Chairman, when Minister spoke about our journey towards becoming a super-aged nation, he highlighted something fundamental, that our people are at the heart of healthcare transformation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I will speak on our approach to workforce and care transformation in healthcare, which is carried out via three pillars.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Second, we build pipeline to ensure manpower sustainability.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: And third, we develop a flexible and agile healthcare system.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Picture this: a patient with diabetes, heart conditions and mobility challenges, juggling multiple appointments across different clinics, each visit requiring time off work, not just for the patient but for the caregiver sometimes, special transport arrangements and often, a caregiver's support to accompany them for these visits.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: It is unsustainable as our population ages and our healthcare needs become more complex.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: How can we meet the rising healthcare needs of an ageing population, improve the care experience while maintaining the quality and standards of care?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Today in a hospital ward, a patient receives coordinated care through a team led by a principal doctor (PD) who is accountable for the patient's overall care plan.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Patients need not be seen by different doctors for each condition, thus reducing the number of referrals to other specialists during their stay.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: And upon discharge, the care of such a patient could then be handed over to their family physician, some of whom are now trained as family medicine specialists, to manage patients with more complex medical conditions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Likewise, team-based care has been introduced in the polyclinics and Primary Care Networks since 2015 and 2018 respectively.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Under such a model, patients with chronic diseases are managed by multi-disciplinary care teams comprising doctors, nurses and care coordinators.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This ensures care continuity and builds the trust between patients and their care team.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Most geriatric dental needs can be managed by polyclinics and CHAS dental clinics.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Specialist care is available for more complex conditions at our hospital dental clinics as well as two national specialty dental centres – the National Dental Centre Singapore and the National University Centre for Oral Health.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Besides transforming our care team in the hospitals and right-siting care to the community, we also want to empower our people to take ownership of their health.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We agree with the vision shared by Dr Haresh Singaraju on how social prescription is integral to preventive care and Healthier SG.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: That is why the Health Plan in Healthier SG includes encouraging patients to adopt lifestyle changes, more exercise and less unhealthy food.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: However, we acknowledge that social prescription is still not commonly adopted, and there are more that we can do together to encourage that.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We will work with community partners to make these interventions available to residents.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In particular for seniors, the network of AACs will support them in this.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Minister of State Rahayu has elaborated earlier in her speech.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In addition, the hospitals also have their respective initiatives in social prescriptions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I also want to assure Mr Pritam Singh that our public hospitals have in place protocols to expedite urgent cases in the Emergency Department, and urgent referrals from primary care to Specialist Outpatient Clinics.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Waiting time alone is not indicative of the quality of medical services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: And in all the top hospitals of the world, patients with more urgent and severe conditions are up-triaged and seen earlier and given necessary resuscitation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Based on several sources, which the Members can also Google, Singapore's healthcare system is consistently ranked within the top 20.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In 2000, the World Health Organization ranked Singapore's sixth best in the world.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Our public health institutions have also consistently been recognised as being one of the best in the world.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In 2026, Newsweek and Statista, a global data platform, ranked the Singapore General Hospital 10th, while the National University of Singapore (NUS) and Tan Tock Seng Hospital are also in the top 100.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Singapore's healthcare system has delivered good health outcomes at an affordable level.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Our life expectancy is about 86 years, as reported by the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation, ahead of many other countries, such as Japan, Switzerland, Australia, South Korea, the United Kingdom (UK) and the US.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This was reported by the World Bank in 2019, and you saw earlier from the charts that Minister has shown that indeed we were able to achieve good health outcomes at a fraction of the cost relative to other countries.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In addition, our hospitals have contingency measures to respond to surge in bed demand.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: These include adding beds, expediting clinically appropriate discharges and deferring non-urgent electives to free up acute capacity for incoming patients.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Even as we augment capacity, our people are at the heart of the healthcare system.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Public healthcare institutions roster staff to ensure adequate rest in between shifts and also monitor the well-being of our staff as they care for our people.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: These are experiences we learnt also from the recent COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Mr Patrick Tay will be pleased to know that MOH has been giving IMH additional funding to enhance the psychiatric services and upgrade its infrastructure for better patient care, to be a leading hub for mental health training and education, and establish its position in tertiary and quaternary mental health research.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: There are also ongoing efforts to enhance psychiatric in-patient, outpatient and crisis care capabilities across our public healthcare institutions to support individuals with both physical and mental health services in the same hospital.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In each of these, care team transformation provides integrated care for patients – promoting team-based care, right-siting of care to the community so that it is more accessible and affordable for our people, and redesigning roles so that professionals are allowed to advance and perform at the apex roles in a safe manner.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The second pillar is to build a sustainable manpower pipeline.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We are working closely with institutes of higher learning (IHLs) to introduce more training pathways to build up a strong local pipeline through Pre-Employment Training.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Mr Cai Yinzhou would be pleased to know that the graduate-entry Master of Science (Audiology) programme at NUS runs biennially and has an average of 13 graduates per cohort.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: For podiatrists, demand is being met through scholarships for local talents to pursue podiatry studies overseas and recruitment of overseas-trained podiatrists.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Unlike the current training model, where an undergraduate needs at least seven years to be qualified as a clinical psychologist, this includes four years for their Bachelor's degree in Psychology, followed by one or two years of work experience before enrolling in the two-year Master of Psychology (Clinical) programme, this new accelerated pathway for undergraduate-to-Masters pathway can be completed in five years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: It would enable aspiring undergraduates, who set their minds fairly early, to be trained as clinical psychologists through a carefully curated curriculum.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This curriculum comprises didactic learning and clinical training during the undergraduate years, developing practitioners with knowledge and skills to care for their patients.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Graduates of this five-year programme will receive both a Bachelor's degree with Honours and a Master's degree.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: NUS' new accelerated undergraduate-to-Masters pathway will complement existing postgraduate training pipelines, including its existing standalone two-year Master of Psychology (Clinical) programme for those with relevant clinical work experience.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Together, these programmes expand our clinical psychologist manpower pipeline to meet increasing mental health needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Healthcare workers remain the bedrock of our healthcare system.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Even as we create new training pathways, we have implemented strategies to improve retention of our healthcare workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We have spoken in this House before about the challenges in attracting and recruiting nurses, especially during the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: While the attrition of nurses has since fallen back to pre-COVID-19 levels of around 7%, we will continue our efforts to encourage more nurses to stay and contribute to the public healthcare system, as well as attract aspiring individuals to build a career in this sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In 2024, we rolled out the Award for Nurses' Grace, Excellence and Loyalty scheme, and reviewed and adjusted nursing salaries in 2025.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: But retention of healthcare workers is not enough to build a robust healthcare system.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We need to continuously upskill our healthcare workforce to take on new and expanded roles.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Healthcare today does not fit neatly into traditional silos.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: A patient with multiple conditions needs professionals who can work seamlessly together.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: That is why we are moving from rigid, specialty-focused training to flexible, competency-based learning delivered via stackable modules in a work-study format where possible.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This reduces time away from work and the impact on patient care.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Separately for mental health, the shared competencies are outlined under the National Mental Health Competency Training Framework to create a "common language" among our AHPs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: With this, our AHPs will be more versatile and able to work more collaboratively to deliver care holistically.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: For nursing, we are working with the polytechnics to redesign existing nursing post-diploma specialty programmes into a work-study format.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This allows the nurses to learn and practise in real-world settings as training is based directly on job activities, enabling nurses to become competent and productive more quickly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Two Advanced Diploma in Nursing programmes – Palliative Care and Community Health – will be prioritised for initial launch in a work-study format.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: With enhanced capabilities, our healthcare workforce is better positioned to deliver comprehensive care.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: These are clinical, clinical neuropsychology, counselling, educational and forensic psychologists.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: MOH and partner Ministries will work with Singapore Psychological Society to raise public awareness of the psychologist professions and support our professionals and stakeholders in navigating the registration process.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The third and last pillar is to develop a flexible and agile healthcare system that can respond to fast-evolving healthcare needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Mental health concerns came to the fore during the COVID-19 pandemic and remains a key national agenda in MOH.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Ms He Ting Ru and Mr Alex Yeo asked about this.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Since the launch of the National Mental Health and Well-being Strategy in 2023, we have established the National Mental Health Office in 2024 to coordinate and oversee multi-agency mental health initiatives.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: First, we have guided mental health service providers to adopt the Tiered Care Model and improve care coordination across different providers, enabling clients to receive seamless care at the most appropriate care setting.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Second, we have expanded the capacity of mental health services across the primary, community, acute and long-term care sectors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Polyclinics and GPs are equipped to provide care to individuals with mild to moderate mental health conditions, such as anxiety and depression.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Community mental health teams provide a range of mental health support to individuals with mental health needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Today, we have 71 Community Outreach Teams (CREST) and 26 Community Intervention Teams (COMIT) to conduct outreach, screening and assessment, psychological intervention and service linkages for seniors with mental health needs or dementia and their caregivers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We have also established the First Stop for Mental Health services to facilitate easy access and navigation of mental health services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Third, we expanded support in encouraging help-seeking amongst youths.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Youths can access CREST-Youth and CHAT, which are sited in the community.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Those who need psychosocial interventions may then be referred to the Youth Integrated Teams.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The recently launched Grovve – spelled g-r-o-v-v-e – at *Scape also provides mental health services to youths where they gather, to improve access and reduce barriers and stigma.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Youth-oriented self-help services, such as Let's Talk and Ask-a-Therapist, can also be accessed on mindline.sg.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In addition to these services, an ecosystem of support is available within the education system.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Educators and staff are trained to look out for signs of distress in students, and refer those who require further support to counsellors in schools or IHLs as well as community mental health professionals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Peer support structures are in place for students to look out for one another and encourage distressed peers to seek help from trusted adults.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Youths are also taught ways to build mental wellness and resilience through the Character and Citizenship Education curriculum in schools and mental well-being programmes in the IHLs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Fifth, we have promoted mental health and wellbeing through educational efforts for the general public, parents and youths through campaigns such as Beyond the Label and resources like Parenting for Wellness and the Positive Use Guide.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Lastly, we have strengthened workplace mental health support in collaboration with the Ministry of Manpower and Workplace Safety and Health Council.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The Well-Being Champions Network has grown from 54 founding member organisations to 800 over the last two years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: As mental health is a complex and multi-faceted issue, we continue to work with various agencies to track and monitor medium- to long-term trends, including overall state of mental health and well-being of our population, for evidence of improvements from the baseline.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We also hear Mr Eric Chua's concerns about our people paying for the silent addiction to explicit materials.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: On this, we recognise that addiction extends beyond individual health to affect families and the broader society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Individuals may also face underlying difficulties such as financial hardship and lack of social support.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We are not just filling positions – we are building a sustainable workforce and system that can adapt, collaborate and deliver good quality care to all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Within the next decade, by 2040, one in three seniors will be aged 80 and above.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: For example, seniors use eight times the amount of hospital care than those who are younger.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: So, I agree with many Members who spoke on the implications.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Today, it is not uncommon to see a working adult supporting elderly parents in their late 60s, who are in turn taking care of their parents in their late 80s.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: I certainly see many of such families in my constituency.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: With family size continuing to shrink, the burden on caregivers will get heavier.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: That is why we want our seniors to remain healthy for as long as possible.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: As the Minister said, it is not just about living longer, but living healthier for longer.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Today, I will outline how we are doing so, with technology as an enabler.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: First, getting seniors to age well in the community.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Third, supporting healthcare providers to deliver better outcomes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: As pointed out by a number of Members, many seniors face social isolation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: A study has estimated that this risk is equivalent to smoking 15 cigarettes a day.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Members would be familiar with the Silver Generation Office (SGO).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Recognising that younger seniors are more digitally savvy, SGO is reaching out this group through the LifeSG app.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Since December last year, over 3,000 seniors have received personalised recommendations on services useful to them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: More than 150 SCCs provide day care services, including for those with dementia and respite care, and over 90 community outreach and intervention teams offer psychosocial support.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Mr Ng Chee Meng, Mr Yip Hon Weng and Mr Fadli Fawzi spoke up for caregivers and referenced what other countries are doing to recognise and support caregivers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Like Members, we believe that caregivers play a vital role and we are doing more to support them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: We are enhancing long-term care subsidies and grants.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: This year, we will raise the per capita household income (PCHI) threshold from $3,600 to $4,800.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: This will cover about seven in 10 households.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Last year, caregivers of over 14,000 seniors benefitted from subsidised home and centre-based respite services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Members also spoke about caregivers who are juggling work and care.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Support is available through various Ministries' effort, for example, Flexible Work Arrangements and the Caregivers Training Grant, which helps to offset costs for training family caregivers and migrant domestic workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Eligible caregivers can also tap on enhanced parental leave provisions such as the new Shared Parental Leave and Unpaid Infant Care Leave.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: We will continue to study Members' suggestions as we explore ways to better support our caregivers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Mr Victor Lye spoke about the unintended consequences of relying on PCHI to assess the caregiving circumstances of families.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: The PCHI means testing approach was discussed at the Budget debate last week.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: However, individuals in difficult circumstances who require additional support can approach our medical social workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Mr Lye gave a few suggestions on how we can improve the current framework.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: MOH will study his suggestions with the Ministry of Finance.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Assoc Prof Terence Ho and Mr Eric Chua advocated for seniors to contribute to the community, including helping fellow seniors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Such involvement gives our seniors a sense of purpose.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Seniors can tap on volunteering opportunities, with some organisations providing training and allowances.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: For example, as Silver Generation Ambassadors, they help conduct outreach to other seniors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Seniors can also join the SG Healthcare Corps to assist with basic patient care.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Those aged 50 and above comprise 20% to 40% of volunteers across these programmes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: We welcome more partners to join this effort.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: I agree with Mr Yip Hong Weng's point that we want our seniors to "leave well", or as the Chinese say, "安然离去".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Since 2023, we have significantly expanded community palliative care services, enhanced subsidies and facilitated hospital discharges at the end of life.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: We want more Singaporeans to spend their final days at home, in an environment where they feel comfortable, surrounded by loved ones.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: As of June 2025, the utilisation rate for home palliative care was around 90%.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: We want to continue supporting families who wish to be with their loved ones at home during their final journey.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Next, I assure Mr Cai Yinzhou and Mr Yip Hong Weng that we do track outcomes of our programmes, such as frailty prevalence, social participation and caregiver well-being.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: We do so with different parties, including research institutions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: They will likely need services from different service providers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: We want their experience to be as seamless as possible and not have to run from pillar to post to receive these services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Technology will be a key enabler for tighter care coordination.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: I agree with Mr Cai's point that we want to make it easier for seniors to access social and health services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: First, we have introduced Integrated Community Care Providers in 84 sub-regions around Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: This means a single party to coordinate care for seniors within each area.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Currently, seniors undergo multiple care assessments done by different service providers they go to.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Not only does this duplicate effort for providers and create greater inconvenience for our seniors, our seniors may also end up with uncoordinated care due to different care plans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Each senior will have a single community care plan developed based on this assessment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Every provider that the senior goes to will take reference from this care plan.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Such an approach will ensure seniors benefit from a seamless experience and better coordinated care.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: We will progressively roll this out from October this year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: We are enabling this new way of coordinating and delivering services through a common IT platform for community care providers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: I refer the Member to Senior Minister of State Koh Poh Koon's recent response to a Parliamentary Question on this matter.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Fundamentally, MOH agrees with the Member to make good use of technology to improve the healthcare experiences for our patients.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: For example, the Productivity and Digitalisation Grant launched in 2022 has supported more than 240 projects, such as systems to automate showering and vital signs monitoring.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: We intend to enhance the grant to make better use of technology solutions in the healthcare sector, including harnessing robotics and AI.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: First, we are working with the vendors for health information management systems used by healthcare providers to comply with the necessary requirements.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Second, we will provide resource guides and training to help healthcare providers and their staff understand and implement these requirements.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: The Grant will offset the cost for providers to onboard the NEHR.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: For typical healthcare providers, this grant will cover up to two years of subscription costs for the health information management systems.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: For providers with in-house systems, the funding support covers up to 40% of enhancement cost.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Most of them already subscribe to a health information management system.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: They can apply and benefit from the NEHR Connect Grant.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: On top of the NEHR Connect Grant, the clinic can receive up to 70% co-funding support from the Cyber Security Agency of Singapore to engage cybersecurity consultants.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: They also benefit from up to 50% funding support from Enterprise Singapore to adopt cybersecurity solutions, such as those for anti-malware.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: In total, the clinic can receive about $20,000 in grants.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: (In Mandarin):   During the Chinese New Year period, when exchanging greetings, I noticed that seniors would say "Gong Xi Fa Cai" less now.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: They understand the importance of maintaining good health, especially after the pandemic.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: To encourage seniors to maintain their physical and mental health, we have established over 230 AACs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: This year we will also designate integrated community care service providers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Care teams will coordinate and plan more comprehensive healthcare according to seniors' needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: For example, if seniors need home personal care services as well as visits to senior care centres, they only need to contact one care team, reducing the hassle of liaising with different community care providers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: We are also actively using technology to provide more precise and convenient care experiences for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: For instance, seniors at risk of falling can enjoy 24-hour smart monitoring under the enhanced home personal care services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: If an accident unfortunately occurs, the system can promptly notify relevant personnel to provide help.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: This way, family members can also have peace of mind.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Through LifeSG, the SGO can interact with seniors and set personalised health plans for them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Since December last year, over 3,000 seniors have benefited.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: This way, doctors can have a more comprehensive understanding of patients' conditions, formulate the most suitable personalised health plans for them and eliminate the need for the patients to repeat their medical histories.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Seniors do not need to worry about remembering the diagnoses or medications that have been prescribed by the doctors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: As the saying goes, "having a senior at home is like having a treasure".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: We will leverage technology to enhance care quality and ensure that seniors receive treatment in a familiar environment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Importantly, a healthcare system that puts people first.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The Minister did not actually address many of the direct questions I had in my speeches, but he did acknowledge that there were many good ideas.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: So, I look forward to seeing some of those perhaps come in future, but I wanted to focus on three clarifications today.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: One is to Minister of State Rahayu on the Woodlands pilot.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: My clarification is how is MOH also working with other agencies to get the most out of this pilot?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is one thing to have the HPB's digital wayfinding to find healthy food options.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: There is another to increase the number of healthy food options, especially halal food options.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And that would require working with, say, the Ministry of National Development.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Because when we have a coffee shop where there is only one halal store and it serves roti prata and mee goreng, and when you depend on those, it is kind of hard to maintain a healthy lifestyle.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: My second clarification is for the Minister on the AI topic.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The consultant in me says, absolutely, yes, fully support the practical use case approach.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The important thing is that these use cases must scale; and some of the things he outlined does that.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But scaling also requires a lot of work on infrastructure, governance and talent that I brought up in my cut speech.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: So, I wonder if he could say something about that.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: My third clarification is also for the Minister, and I am happy to hear about the changes to MediSave500/700, or now we call it MediSave chronic and MediSave preventive care.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It was actually entirely the crux of my suggestion on MediSave flex for that purpose.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I will start with the second question, AI scaling.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, I do not have much to add, but I think Ms Mariam Jaafar is also aware of all the steps we have taken, and she mentioned that in her cut.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In terms of IT infrastructure, NEHR, Next Generation Electronic Medical Records, HEALIX, AI Medical Imaging Platform for Singapore public healthcare.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We set up all this quietly in the background, and then at the same time, strengthened cybersecurity.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, a lot of background work has been done.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We are now, therefore, in a position where we are ready to say if a use case proves to be useful in a hospital in a particular sandbox, we can scale it up.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And I think we are ready to do that now in a very proactive way.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As for MediSave, it is difficult to do modelling.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But the fact is, the needs across the population are so different.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Sometime back, we gave an answer in Parliament how much MediSave is left at the point of demise for someone aged 85 and above, when they die.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And so, we collated the data from 2017 to 2021.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It depends on who we are talking about.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Those with less than $1,000, I think is barely enough.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We really need to save their MediSave towards their old age.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, I think some Members have raised this suggestion: can we have a bit more flexibility based on balances?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Can we free up the rules a bit?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is conceptually correct, but it is not so easy.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is not a matter of modelling, but being able to cater to individual circumstances.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For a scheme that applies to the whole population, it is never easy to do precise policy.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Since I am standing here, I will answer on behalf of Minister of State Rahayu.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Working with other agencies in the community for the north, we might be thinking of different things.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But what we are thinking about is actually a care model, not so much just food.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But a care model where we encourage residents to do early check-ups, enrol for Healthier SG, with the support of a CHP that makes things very easy, a very convenient touchpoint that, together, with local Members of Parliament and advisors, we can make sure that more people respond to our preventive care push.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: One is on team-based care, as the Senior Minister of State has mentioned, that it has been around since 2015, and that is something which the clusters have done great works and set up frameworks for.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Yet many of the services, nurse-led, pharmacist-led, allied health-led services are underutilised.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: And second, is on the aspect of Healthier SG enrolment, where we have had residents who have enrolled across public and private.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Have we studied the factors to strengthen that relationship such that patients do not drift across?

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: On the first question of team-based care and whether certain AHP-led services are underutilised.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We acknowledge that this is one of the challenges we have to continue to deal with, because patients do have autonomy on who they eventually want the care to be given.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, it is not something that we can do to force person to see a particular professional.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: And that is why, building rapport is important.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: At the same time, we are also signalling that these are professionals that have been trained, given accredited certification to perform at a higher level.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: And over time, we hope that the lived experience of patients who have seen these professionals will validate some of the outcomes that patients are looking for, so that over time we build confidence, build rapport in the community, and patients will gradually accept the kind of referral pathways that we are channelling to.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: One of the things that we are doing in the CHP is to have more nurses actually now fronting many of the conversations for our seniors.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: It is a good way to socialise to our seniors and our patients that the nurse can deliver many of the care that they already need.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, it will take multiple approach to do this and it will take some time as well.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But increasingly, we are also seeing that this capacity will be better utilised by the population.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The second question on enrolment across the different providers, especially in Healthier SG, that indeed is something that we have to continue to work on.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Because beyond enrolment is also how well the clients or the patients follow-up with what is needed in the implementation of the care plan.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, we are under no illusion that just because we roll out Healthier SG, everything will be very smooth right at the beginning.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: It takes a bit of, not just system change in the providers, in the doctors and the care teams, but also, a gradual shift in the mindset of our population as well.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, it is something that we have to continue to do.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: There is no magic bullet to this and it is not something we can achieve overnight.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Because there may be a time lapse risk-reduction treatment for a healthy breast versus a breast that has already cancer detected and this will be supplemental cost throughout the life course of an individual.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: What we do is that we take guidance and recommendations from the Screening Test Review Committee as well as the Agency for Care Effectiveness Clinical Guidelines.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: So, there are some evidence and data that we will use in determining these protocols.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: But what the Member has raised will be something we will take back and will consider to be included.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Mr Chairman, I thank the Minister for his comprehensive response.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In Tengah, Singapore's newest town with many young families, something quite remarkable is happening.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Since last year, I have met 19 sets of twins among residents there.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It reflects the stage of life many couples in Tengah are in as they begin building their families.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As the Minister noted, healthcare needs for younger population are often episodic.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But towns, like Tengah, also gives us a rare opportunity to start prevention early.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Could the Minister share how MOH is working with other agencies so that preventive health can be built into new towns, like Tengah, right from the start, rather than introduce only when populations have already aged?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Some of the basic steps — It is like a fruit tree.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: After that, ensure that they follow up with their check-ups, with their vaccinations, with their health screening.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It will help if the Member promotes anti-smoking, enforce against vapes.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: All these are very basic steps to ensure good health.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The first relates to the new accelerated pathway for clinical psychologists.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: So, my clarification is, what is the projected increase in the number of entrants to the profession as a result of this, in the future?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: My next clarification relates to the announcement of the registration of psychologists.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I want to thank MOH for announcing this.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I know there are a lot of people in the profession who actually really anticipate this, and they are very happy to hear this.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I have two clarifications relating to this, and they were actually part of my cut.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The first is, what is the support for people who are aspiring to enter the profession?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Because as I mentioned, the practicums and the supervision costs can be quite prohibitive.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: My clarification relates to what is the Ministry doing, or how is the Ministry looking to address some of the concerns about barriers to entry for professionals who are interested in entering the professions?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And then, the second point is, for people who are actually seeking these services, for clients, what support is available if they have, in the meantime before these registration requirements come in, what recourse do they have and what support do they have if they have concerns about professional ethics and standards?

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: On the first question about how many psychologists will end up eventually in the system and what does the new pathway mean in terms of increasing the headcounts, I would say it is probably very hard to tell at the moment.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, we will also see what the uptake is from the first intake of the course.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But bear in mind that there is also a pathway for existing psychologists to upgrade.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We need to actually just sense out what is the demand overall from the undergraduates as well as the in-service psychologists over time.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The challenge also is because we have not done registration of psychologists before this.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But in time to come, once the registration is done, we will have a better grasp of the situation.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: On the second question of what support will be given to the aspiring students who may want to enter the course, we are still in the midst of discussing with the institutions.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, if you are a Singaporean student, you will expect that there will be some subsidies to the fees.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The third question on how can the public, who may want to seek psychological care, know who is legitimate.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In the meantime, before registration, it will be very hard for us to provide a detailed list of the individual specialists or psychologists.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But perhaps, what they can do is to check whether this individual is registered, at least for the moment, with the Singapore Psychological Society.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Because at least, that is the community of practice that is recognised as peers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, that will be a place to start for now.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But certainly, for those psychologists who are practising in our public healthcare institutions, there is already a governance framework in place and the public should at least be comforted that these are the ones that have already been under supervision and recognised by our public healthcare institutions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: One pertains to my cut on healthcare manpower.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I also note the comments made by various officeholders about the super-aged society that we are here now.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In line with this, is the Ministry looking at new indicators or data points with regard to how the healthcare system is working in this new environment?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, we have got healthcare institution statistics, which MOH helpfully releases now, attendance at emergency medicine departments, time for admission to wards and bed occupancy rates.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But could there be other indicators that also would be helpful for the public, for example, waiting times at polyclinics?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And would there be other indicators that reflect on how well the healthcare system is doing, looking after, especially given the new environment that we are in?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My second clarification deals with the other cut I had about the additional withdrawal limits.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I take the Minister's point about MediSave and the karma of MediSave, that there will always be greater demands on it to deal with expenditures.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But, of course, with the basic healthcare sum also increasing year-on-year, this would be inevitable to some extent.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To that end, can I enquire whether there would be some consideration as to increasing the additional withdrawal limits through MediSave as well?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I will put Mr Pritam Singh's suggestion into our wish list, which is getting quite long.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But all these are done in the context of ensuring subsidised healthcare is affordable and minimising out-of-pocket expenses for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As for the Member's first question, there are so many indicators in MOH.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If the Member files a Parliamentary Question, I will have so many indicators to tell him that we are monitoring and that includes waiting times, Emergency Departments, polyclinics, bed occupancy rates, average length of stay across different settings.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
